young.html: Henry James was an American writer who spent most of his life in England. He wrote long, careful sentences about what people think and feel but don't say out loud.

In The Beast in the Jungle, a man named John Marcher is sure that something huge and strange is going to happen to him someday, like a wild beast waiting to jump out of the jungle. His friend May Bartram promises to watch and wait with him. They wait for years and years. Marcher is so busy waiting for his big event that he never notices the most important thing right beside him: May's friendship and love. When he finally understands, it is too late.

young.cap: Step through the years of Marcher's waiting.

young.html: Notice today. Marcher missed what was right in front of him. Tonight at dinner, each person names one good thing that happened today that they almost didn't notice: a kind word, a funny moment, a sunset.

full.html: Henry James (1843–1916) was born in New York, the brother of the philosopher William James, whose Principles of Psychology appears earlier on this ladder. Henry settled in England in 1876 and became a British subject in 1915. His novels, such as The Portrait of a Lady and The Ambassadors, often set Americans among Europeans. The Beast in the Jungle is a long story published in his collection The Better Sort (1903).

At a country house called Weatherend, John Marcher meets May Bartram again. She reminds him that ten years before, in Italy, he told her his secret: he has always felt that he is being kept for some rare and strange event, perhaps a terrible one, that will one day break upon him.

full.text: Something or other lay in wait for him, amid the twists and the turns of the months and the years, like a crouching Beast in the Jungle.
full.author: Henry James
full.work: The Beast in the Jungle, chapter II
full.ed: The Better Sort (first published 1903); text of the Martin Secker edition, London

full.html: May agrees to wait and watch with him. Years pass in quiet visits, theater evenings and birthday gifts. Marcher thinks it would be selfish to marry while he is waiting for his fate. May grows ill. Before she dies, she tells him, gently, that the thing has already happened, and that he hasn't noticed.

Long afterward, at May's grave, Marcher sees a stranger whose face is raw with grief for someone he has lost. Suddenly Marcher understands. His fate was to be the one man who never loved, though love had been offered to him for years:

full.text: The fate he had been marked for he had met with a vengeance—he had emptied the cup to the lees; he had been the man of his time, the man, to whom nothing on earth was to have happened.
full.author: Henry James
full.work: The Beast in the Jungle, chapter VI
full.ed: The Better Sort (first published 1903); text of the Martin Secker edition, London

full.name: gb-james-waiting
full.cap: The years of waiting, our summary.

full.html: The "beast" is not an outside disaster. It is the empty life that comes from waiting for something grand instead of living, and loving, now.

James tells the whole story from inside Marcher's mind, so we see only what he sees. The reader may notice May's feelings long before Marcher does. That gap between what the hero knows and what we can guess is the story's quiet engine.
Expecting a jungle adventure. There is no jungle and no animal: the title is Marcher's own image for his fate.

items: William James, Henry's brother, described the "stream of consciousness"; Henry wrote fiction that follows a mind from within, a method that Woolf and Joyce, later in this era, carried further.
Sophocles' Oedipus is another hero who learns the truth about himself too late.
Beckett's Waiting for Godot turns waiting itself into a play.
Proust, in Swann in Love, also studies a man who misreads his own heart.
Is it possible to waste a life by waiting for it to start?
Why doesn't May simply tell Marcher what she feels?
Was Marcher's fate fixed, or did he choose it, day by day?
What does it mean to really pay attention to another person?

questions: Marcher waited his whole life for something big. Have you ever waited so hard for one thing that you missed another?
Why do you think May agreed to wait with him?
What is the "beast" in the end?
Should May have told Marcher what she knew? Why might she have stayed quiet?
How can we notice the people who care about us?
